# JSVM

Version 0.1.3 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

PocketOne's JS engine for `pb_hooks` and `pb_migrations`. It runs the same JS API as PocketBase (`$app`, `onX`,
`routerAdd`, `cronAdd`, `$http`, `$security`, ...) on QuickJS, with one VM per app:

- **Real globals.** Every hook file runs in the app's one global scope, so top-level helpers, constants and state are
  visible to every handler. No more `require()` inside each handler.
- **ES modules.** `*.pb.mjs` (and TypeScript `*.pb.ts`/`*.pb.mts`) hook files and modules use `import`/`export`,
  including top-level `await`; `*.pb.js` and `*.pb.cjs` stay scripts with `require()`. Both share the same module
  instances.
- **TypeScript.** `.ts`, `.mts` and `.cts` hooks, migrations and modules run directly (types stripped by esbuild,
  linked into the binary), with error positions in your `.ts` source.
- **Async.** Handlers can be `async`. Every Go function has an `.async(...)` twin that runs off the VM and returns a
  promise, so one app serves other requests while it waits: `await $app.findRecordById.async("posts", id)`.
- **Timers.** `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearTimeout`, `clearInterval` and `queueMicrotask`, as in browsers and
  Node.js. A timer set while serving a request is cleared once the request is answered or its client goes away.
- **Cancellation.** `AbortController`, `AbortSignal` (`timeout`, `abort`, `any`) and `DOMException`, as in browsers.
  `fn.asyncWith({ signal }, ...args)` is an `.async` call a signal can stop, and a Go function that takes a
  `context.Context` sees it cancelled.
- **Hard limits per app.** A memory cap (JS heap plus Go objects JS holds), a CPU and a wall-clock budget per task, and
  caps on queued tasks and async calls. A runaway script stops with an error; other apps in the process keep running.
- **Real error positions.** Stack traces name `pb_hooks/<file>:<line>`.

Every PocketOne app runs on it: a standalone app or an instance on a multisite host, whatever the runtime. PocketBase's
own `plugins/jsvm` (goja) is for pure PocketBase compatibility only: `jsvm: goja` under `app:` in `pocketone.yaml` (or
`--jsvm goja`) runs a standalone app on it, with pages, `$mcp`, `$apiTokens`, `$bulkmail` and JS contracts off.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

The engine is pure Go (QuickJS translated to Go by [modernc.org/libquickjs](https://pkg.go.dev/modernc.org/libquickjs),
the way PocketBase uses modernc.org/sqlite), so it needs no cgo: `CGO_ENABLED=0` builds and cross-compiles work as with
stock PocketBase. In your own Go build, register it where you'd register `plugins/jsvm`:

```go
jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", MigrationsDir: "pb_migrations"})
```

The module is `pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm`.

## Configure

`Config` takes PocketBase's jsvm fields (`HooksDir`, `HooksWatch`, `HooksFilesPattern`, `MigrationsDir`,
`MigrationsFilesPattern`, `TypesDir`; `HooksPoolSize` is accepted and ignored) plus:

- `OnInit func(rt js.Runtime)`: add globals after everything else is set up.
- `VM`: the limits. `MemoryLimit` (JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds, default 64 MiB), `TaskBudget` (JS time per
  stretch, default 5 s), `TaskWall` (wall time per stretch, sync Go calls included, default 30 s), `AwaitLimit` (a
  whole async handler, awaits included, default 15 min), `WaitTimeout` (a handler's synchronous part, queue wait
  included, default 30 s), `QueueSize`, `MaxAsync`, `MaxTimers` (timers pending at once, default 1024), `MaxPumpDepth`. A stretch is the JS between two `await`s, so
  time spent awaiting an `.async` call counts only toward `AwaitLimit`. Past `AwaitLimit`, or when the HTTP request a
  handler serves ends (the client went away), the call fails and the handler stops at its next `await`: async calls it
  started are dropped when they finish and new ones throw. A detached promise outlives its handler. A timer belongs to
  the call that set it: each run is a task of its own (its own `TaskBudget` and `TaskWall`), it's cleared when that
  call is given up, and for a request also when the request is answered. Timers set at the top of a file run until
  cleared. The `pocketone`
  binary sets `memory`, `task_time`, `task_wall` and `await_time` in `pocketone.yaml`'s `app: js_limits:`
  ([QuickJS hooks](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs#6-memory-and-time-limits)).
  Array methods that walk every index (`join`, `indexOf`, `slice`, `forEach`, `concat`, `flat`, ...) and arrays passed
  to Go throw a `RangeError` past `MemoryLimit / 16` elements: QuickJS doesn't check `TaskBudget` inside those loops,
  and a sparse array (`new Array(1e9)`) or array-like costs no memory, so the cap is what stops them. No dense array
  that long fits in `MemoryLimit`.
- `Extensions`: values that extend it (below).

## Use

Write hooks and migrations as in PocketBase's [JS docs](https://pocketbase.io/docs/js-overview/); they run unchanged.
What's new:

```js
// pb_hooks/main.pb.js
const cache = new Map()

routerAdd("GET", "/post/{slug}", async (e) => {
	const slug = e.request.pathValue("slug")
	if (!cache.has(slug)) {
		cache.set(slug, await e.app.findFirstRecordByData.async("posts", "slug", slug))
	}
	return e.json(200, cache.get(slug))
})
```

- Hook files run before the app opens its database, as in PocketBase, so a `$app` query at a file's top level fails.
  Read data in `onBootstrap` after `e.next()`, or in a handler:

  ```js
  let users = null
  onBootstrap((e) => {
  	e.next()
  	users = e.app.findCollectionByNameOrId("users")
  })
  ```
- Globals live as long as the app's VM. A restart, a hooks reload or running out of memory starts a fresh one, so keep
  durable data in the database.
- After an `await`, other requests may have run: use `e.app`, not the global `$app`, and keep transactions short across
  `await`s (they hold SQLite's write lock).
- Use `.async` for anything slow (`$http.send`, `sleep`, slow queries). Without it, other requests still run while a
  call waits, but they nest on one stack and wait on each other: under load, a plain `sleep(100)` served 19 requests a
  second where `await sleep.async(100)` served 481 ([benchmark](https://pocketone.dev/docs/quickjs#how-it-performs)).
- `process.env` and a small `Buffer` (`from`, `toString` with utf8, base64, hex) are there.

### Cancelling Go calls

A Go function whose first parameter is a `context.Context` gets one from the engine; JS passes only the other
arguments (or a Go context of its own, such as `e.request.context()`, first). The context is cancelled when the
request or hook the call runs for is given up (its client went away, `AwaitLimit` passed) and when the VM closes,
so abandoned work stops instead of running on. Answering the request doesn't cancel it: background work keeps going.

To bound or cancel one call, pass an `AbortSignal` to `asyncWith`:

```js
// a model call that gives up after a minute, even in background work after the response was sent
const reply = await callModel.asyncWith({ signal: AbortSignal.timeout(60_000) }, prompt)

// or cancel it yourself, or whichever comes first
const c = new AbortController()
const signal = AbortSignal.any([AbortSignal.timeout(60_000), c.signal])
```

When the signal aborts, the promise rejects at once with `signal.reason`: a `DOMException` named `"TimeoutError"`
for `AbortSignal.timeout`, `"AbortError"` for `controller.abort()`, or the reason you gave `abort(reason)`. The Go
function's context is cancelled with a cause that wraps `jsvm.ErrAborted`. A signal that has already aborted rejects
without calling Go. A Go function that takes no context can't be stopped: its promise is let go and the call runs to
its end (still counted against `MaxAsync`).

`AbortSignal.timeout` runs on a Go timer that keeps going after the request is answered, where `setTimeout` is
refused, and it is dropped when the call is given up. Like a timer, it counts against `MaxTimers` until it fires.

### Modules: import and require

Name a file for what it is: `.mjs` is an ES module, `.cjs` is CommonJS. A plain `.js` file is CommonJS, so existing
PocketBase hooks run unchanged (inside `node_modules`, Node's rule applies: `"type": "module"` in the package's
`package.json` makes its `.js` files ES modules). TypeScript is written as ES modules, so `.ts` and `.mts` are ES
modules and `.cts` is the CommonJS exception.

| File | Runs as | Shares through |
|---|---|---|
| `pb_hooks/*.pb.mjs`, `*.pb.ts`, `*.pb.mts` | ES module: `import`, `export`, top-level `await`, `import.meta` | `export` / `import`; its top-level names are private |
| `pb_hooks/*.pb.js`, `*.pb.cjs`, `*.pb.cts` | script in the app's one global scope, with `require()` | globals |
| `pb_migrations/*.mjs`, `*.ts`, `*.mts` | ES module | each migration has its own scope either way |
| `pb_migrations/*.js`, `*.cjs`, `*.cts` | script in its own function scope | |

All of them run in the app's one VM: scripts and modules share the global object (a module can read a script's
globals) and one instance of every module.

```js
// pb_hooks/lib/store.mjs
export const state = { hits: 0 }
export const bump = () => ++state.hits

// pb_hooks/main.pb.mjs
import { bump } from "./lib/store.mjs"
import legacy from "./lib/legacy.cjs"      // CommonJS: module.exports is the default export
import { hello } from "some-package"       // node_modules, CommonJS or ES
const { greeting } = await import("./lib/greeting.mjs")      // top-level await: done before the app serves

routerAdd("GET", "/hit", (e) => e.json(200, { hits: bump() }))
```

- `import` and `require()` resolve the same way: relative paths (`.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.json` and `index.*`
  tried in turn), then `node_modules` packages by `package.json` `exports` (the `import` or `require` condition) or
  `main`.
- A module loads once per app, however many files import or require it, so its state is shared by every request.
  Importing a CommonJS module gives its `module.exports` as the default export, its keys as named exports, and the same
  instance `require()` returns.
- `require()` of an ES module returns its namespace (the same instance `import` gives), as in Node 22, as long as the
  module has no top-level `await`; for one that does, use `await import("./lib/x.mjs")`.

### TypeScript

`.ts`, `.mts` and `.cts` files run as they are: esbuild strips the types when the file loads, and each file's source
map is kept, so an error names `pb_hooks/main.pb.mts:12:5` in your source, not in the stripped code.

- There's no type checking at runtime. Check with `tsc --noEmit` or your editor; `types.d.ts` and `tsconfig.json`
  in the project root type the whole JS API.
- Imports may name the compiled file, as TypeScript's `NodeNext` style does: `import { add } from "./math.js"` loads
  `math.ts` when there's no `math.js`.
- `import type` and other type-only imports disappear, so a `*.pb.cts` script can use them and stay a script.
- A `.cts` module may still be written with `import`/`export`; it's turned into CommonJS.

### Types

When the app starts, `types.d.ts` in the project root (the folder holding `pb_hooks`, next to `pb_data` and
`pocketone.yaml`) gets the declarations of the whole JS API, for your editor and `tsc`:

- PocketBase's API generated from PocketOne's core (its extra hooks included), by PocketBase's own generator.
- What this engine adds ([`pocketone.d.ts`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/jsvm/pocketone.d.ts)): `.async` and `.asyncWith` on every Go function, fully
  typed (`await $app.findRecordById.async(...)` is a `Promise<core.Record>`, and a `context.Context` first parameter
  is left out), `AbortController`/`AbortSignal`, `require`, `process`, `Buffer`, `console`, `import.meta`.
- Each extension's own API, for the extensions on in that app (`$mcp`, `$apiTokens`, `$bulkmail`, `onContracts` and
  the contracts' action hooks).

Beside it, the app writes a `tsconfig.json` when the folder has none, so your editor and `tsc --noEmit` work right
away. It's yours from then on: the app never overwrites it.

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "Bundler",
    "lib": ["ES2022"],
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["types.d.ts", "pb_hooks/**/*", "pb_migrations/**/*", "pb_pages/**/*"]
}
```

`skipLibCheck` skips two type errors inside PocketBase's own generated declarations. Commit both files: a fresh
checkout is then typed before the app first runs, and a diff in `types.d.ts` shows what an upgrade or a new extension
changed in the JS API. Empty hook files get a `/// <reference path="../types.d.ts" />` line.

`Config.TypesDir` puts both somewhere else. With hooks embedded in the binary ([Bundle](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bundle)) and
no `TypesDir`, neither is written. In a PocketOne checkout,
`go generate` in `ext/jsvm` regenerates the declarations after a core change (the `TestTypes` tests fail until you
do).

## Integrations

Extensions plug in through `Config.Extensions` with the engine-neutral types in
[`ext/extkit/js`](https://github.com/pocketonehq/pocketone/blob/main/ext/extkit/js/js.go). A value implements any of:

- `OnInit(rt)`: set up the VM. `BindJS(app, rt)`: expose a Go API. `TypeScript()`: declare it for editors and
  `tsc` (appended to `types.d.ts`). `FilterTypes(decl)`: change the finished declarations (the sandbox
  declares what it hides `never`).
- `OnCall(rt)`: wrap every handler call; an error refuses it.
- `HTTPClient(rt)`: the client `$http.send` uses.
- `HookFiles`, `MigrationFiles`, `Modules`: hooks, migrations and `require()` modules from somewhere other than disk.
- `OnLoad(rt, root, file, content)`: wrap loading each hook file.

`js.Run(app, fn)` runs Go code on the app's VM; a `js.Func` kept from JS can be called from any goroutine.

A binding whose calls should be cancellable takes `ctx context.Context` as its Go function's first parameter and
hands the caller's `{ signal }` to `asyncWith` in its prelude. `asyncWith` reads only `options.signal`, and a missing
one makes it a plain `.async`, so a wrapper can pass the caller's options object as is:

```js
// Go: n.Set("call", func(ctx context.Context, kind, op, opts string) (string, error) { ... })
const callAsync = async (kind, op, o) => {
  const { signal, ...rest } = o ?? {}
  return JSON.parse(await n.call.asyncWith({ signal }, kind, op, JSON.stringify(rest)))
}
```

The same function called without `.async` gets the handler's context, so one Go function serves both. Under goja
(`jsvm: goja`) neither `asyncWith` nor the supplied context exists.

[Bundle](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bundle) uses these to serve hooks and migrations embedded in the binary.

## Example

```go
// Command example serves example/pb_hooks with the jsvm extension: one QuickJS VM for the app, so the hook file's
// top-level helpers and state are visible to every handler.
//
//	cd example && go run . serve
//	curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hello/world
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/devusers"
	"pocketone.dev/ext/jsvm"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app)
	jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", MigrationsDir: "pb_migrations"})
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## How it works

- Each app's VM is owned by one goroutine, its loop; everything that touches the VM runs there. Go code
  elsewhere posts tasks and waits. A Go call made from JS that fires a hook runs it inline, so Go → JS → Go → JS works.
- Go values cross live through two QuickJS classes: `GoObject` (property get/set/has/keys go to Go by reflection, with
  PocketBase's JS names) and `GoFunc` (calls go to Go). Each holds a handle into the VM's table; QuickJS's refcounting
  frees it as soon as JS drops it.
- Memory: QuickJS caps its own heap. Go objects JS holds are charged to the same budget: a per-type estimate, and a
  reachability walk for fresh results of Go calls.
- QuickJS is [modernc.org/libquickjs](https://pkg.go.dev/modernc.org/libquickjs), Bellard's QuickJS translated to Go,
  so there is no cgo. It runs about as fast as goja; deep recursion stops at `VM.StackSize` (QuickJS stack slots,
  about one per call; default 5000) with "InternalError: stack overflow".
- Benchmarks and the red team (27 attacks against 50 VMs in one process) are in the package's tests
  (`ASYNCVM_BENCH=1`, `ASYNCVM_REDTEAM=1`).
